title: New Cough Syrup (BronchSure)
prompt: Your client is a pharmaceutical company that has recently launched a new cough syrup called BronchSure, and they want your help in determining the appropriate pricing.

facts.reveal: A mid-sized Indian pharmaceutical company operating pan-India. Strong networks in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Delhi NCR and Karnataka; weaker in the East and South.
A metro-first launch across chemists, modern trade and e-commerce.
Over the counter in most states; in a few states it is behind the counter, dispensed by the pharmacist.

Four branded over-the-counter syrups dominate, with multiple private-label generics, Ayurvedic syrups and home remedies. Hospitals and bulk buyers purchase multi-pack tendered generics from distributors.

facts.asks: Competitor price, only if the candidate proposes a figure near it
facts.reveal: Yes, ₹100–120 per 100 ml is a fair estimate.

Capture meaningful market share within 18 months while ensuring sustainable margins. Secondary: sign hospital and school tenders in metros and build over-the-counter brand presence in urban pharmacies. Profitability matters but is secondary in the initial year.

facts.asks: What is different about the product
facts.reveal: Moderate but meaningful differentiation: a mixed formulation (an antitussive plus a mucolytic), lower sedation, a paediatric sugar-free variant, good shelf stability and no cold chain.
There are regulatory constraints; extremely high pricing is not practical.

Variable cost is about ₹30 per 100 ml bottle. Fixed cost is about ₹8 crore of marketing in the first year, of which ₹6 crore is for BronchSure. The forecast is 5 lakh bottles in year 1, subject to seasonal fluctuation.
Yes. If early traction is strong, they can produce and distribute up to 10 lakh bottles in year 1.

acceptedAssumptions: Strong brands at ₹150–180; private-label generics below ₹90
outOfScope: Exact competitor prices beyond the confirmed band

crux.statement: At the base forecast, cost per bottle (₹150) sits above the mid-range market (₹100–120). The price only works if volume scales, so the share objective and the scale-up are the same lever. Value-based pricing is weak here because over-the-counter buyers cannot verify the clinical edge.
crux.clue: The share objective, then the question "is the company open to scaling?"

paths: Cost-based with a competitor check (the source's route)
Competitor-based first, with cost as the floor

wrongTurns.text: Cost-plus at ₹150 without noticing it is above the market

quant.working: Base case: ₹6 crore ÷ 5 lakh bottles = ₹120 fixed + ₹30 variable = ₹150 a bottle. At 10 lakh bottles: ₹60 + ₹30 = ₹90. With a 30–35% margin on price: 90 ÷ 0.70 ≈ ₹128.6 and 90 ÷ 0.65 ≈ ₹138.5, so about ₹130.
quant.answer: ₹150 a bottle at 5 lakh; ₹90 at 10 lakh; a launch price of about ₹130

answerKey: A launch price of about ₹130 per 100 ml: above the mid-range, below premium
The price depends on reaching the 10 lakh volume; say what happens if it does not

close.condition: The candidate has both per-unit costs and a price with a competitor check.
close.prompt: What price do you recommend, and why?

anchors.s5: Picks a method without data; arithmetic slips.
anchors.s7: Works out both per-unit costs and lands a defensible price with a competitor check.
anchors.s9: Sees that the base-case cost is above the market, ties the scale-up to the share goal, and raises channel margins and the tender segment.

verifierFlags.decision: Use "mid-sized"; the summary page says the same. "Top 5" is dropped.

verifierFlags.text: The ₹150–180 strong-brand and below-₹90 generic bands come from the candidate, not the interviewer.
verifierFlags.decision: Kept as accepted assumptions. The interviewer confirms only the ₹100–120 mid-range band.

verifierFlags.text: The source treats manufacturer price as the retail price, though distributor and retailer margins would sit on top.
verifierFlags.decision: Keep the book's logic: ₹130 is the retail price. Raising channel margins is credited at the top anchor.
